output.headline: UK and EU near wide-ranging deal, with fees and industry access the final hurdles
output.bodyHtml:
Britain and the EU are nearing a deal to be struck at a Brussels summit this month, with ministers now weighing whether to go further still: offering to spend as much as £450m a year giving EU students the same discounted university fees as British students, in exchange for UK access to the bloc’s Made in Europe industrial programme, the Guardian has learned.

Government sources say ministers have drawn up plans to let students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, and are prepared to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities for the change.

Related: Rachel Reeves says UK’s future is in EU as she backs Andy Burnham on Brexit

On Sunday, the former chancellor Rachel Reeves praised the prime minister, Andy Burnham, for his willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe, saying she believed Britain’s future lay within the EU. In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.

In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”.

Ministers hope that, if such an agreement is reached at the Brussels summit, it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off.

Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months, to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU, and to lay out options for how the relationship could develop in future, including full re-entry.

British officials say, however, that they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed industrial scheme, which will otherwise impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc.

Giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially at a time when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans.

One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.”

A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”

The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers.

British access to the Made in Europe scheme, due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities, are the two remaining hurdles.

Reports suggest up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study under the youth mobility scheme, after EU member states had originally pushed for between 100,000 and 150,000 places, with some arguing for no quota at all.

EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiations to a standstill this year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks.

The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday, with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore restoring the UK’s access to EU databases.

EU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK, as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states.

Member states are pushing for firm language on fees, while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. France dropped its opposition to the UK’s inclusion in the Industrial Accelerator Act, with a proposal that any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved, as long as it dynamically aligned on trade measures.

Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the fees discussion from the joint statement at the summit entirely, deferring any agreement for six months. But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement that would allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”.

Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discount for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses.

Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that, under the most expensive scenario – reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and assuming very high demand – the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”.

Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, has previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course.

UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme.

The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme, prompting warnings from the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – previously the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position, proposing to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs.

That could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, recently told the Guardian he would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels.

The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements.

The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out the text. Despite a last-minute cancellation, officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission have continued the work.
output.standfirst: Britain and the EU are nearing agreement on emissions trading, farm goods and youth mobility, with ministers weighing a £450m plan to cut EU students' fees in return for access to the bloc's industrial scheme
output.progress: Negotiators are working to finalise a joint statement for EU ambassadors this week, ahead of the 20 November summit.

output.headline: Bringing heating back to 0.8C could save most of the world's glaciers
output.bodyHtml:
Global heating should be brought back down to below 1C after an inevitable period of overshooting international climate targets, in order to limit dangerous and irreversible melting in Earth’s icy regions, a UN report has found.

The cryosphere – Earth’s water in frozen form, including all its ice and snow – is so sensitive to extreme heat that temperatures must stay above the 1.5C threshold for as short a period as possible, the scientists urged. They said enough planet-heating carbon should be removed from the atmosphere to bring long-term warming down much further still, ideally below 1C by 2150.

Last month, a separate UNEP report found the world must cut emissions by 18% by 2030 and by 45% by 2035 to have a good chance of keeping temperatures from rising more than 1.7C above preindustrial levels, warning there were “no good outcomes” of remaining above 1.5C for long.

The cryosphere report comes as world leaders and diplomats converge on Turkey for the 31st annual Cop climate conference. It documents rapid and accelerating melting of the cryosphere and polar oceans, with damage ranging from the loss of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, driving sea level rises that threaten hundreds of millions of people, to thawing permafrost, which releases yet more planet-heating gas.

Permanent and widespread losses of snow and ice expose a “persistent myth” that overshooting the 1.5C target of the Paris climate agreement – to 2C or 3C – could be manageable or even preferable to urgent cuts to emissions, the report found.

The planet has heated by 1.3C since pre-industrial times, and failures to curb greenhouse gas emissions and protect nature have led scientists to conclude that some level of overshoot is now inevitable as they fight to keep end-of-century warming to 1.5C.

The cryosphere report found that current policies, which are on course for 2.8C of global heating, would reduce glacier ice mass to below 10% in the Rockies, Alps, Iceland and Scandinavia. If warming were limited to 1.5C, about 20-35% of that mass would remain.

In the Hindu Kush Himalayas, where glaciers are a source of water for nearly a quarter of humanity, current policies would leave just 41% of the ice mass intact. If warming were limited to 1.5C, 83% would remain.

Glaciers, which are still responding to historical warming, would preserve about 70% of their current volume over a timescale of centuries if long-term heating were brought back down to 0.8C, the report found.

Related: Slovenia mourns loss of glacier on its highest peak after scorching summer

The report, written by 80 scientists brought together by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative (ICCI) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), found much of the damage would be permanent even if global temperatures were brought back down to 1.5C, including glacier melt that raises sea levels and threatens water security.

Meanwhile, the ice sheets covering Greenland and Antarctica, which are melting about six times faster today than in the 1990s, would continue to lose ice even in scenarios where overshoot is brief and temperatures return to 1.5C, the report found. The scientists said a safe, long-term temperature limit for polar ice sheets lies much closer to 1.0C of global heating, and possibly even lower.

James Kirkham, a glaciologist at ICCI and the lead author of the report, said the cryosphere is “one of the most sensitive components of the climate system”, and the consequences of its loss affect the whole planet.

Related: The threatening thaw: climate professor on heatwave risks to tipping point of permafrost

The high overshoot expected under current policies – with peak temperatures of about 3C – would thaw nearly all near-surface permafrost, make “severe and possibly abrupt” disruption to ocean circulation likely, and lead to widespread acidification, the report found. The latest scientific research suggests sea ice recovers more slowly than previously thought.

“Snow and ice respond rapidly to every fraction of a degree of warming,” said Kirkham. “But most of these systems will take centuries or millennia to recover after overshoot, especially if tipping points are crossed that cause changes to become essentially irreversible.”

“This year, we’ve already seen one of the largest and most deadly ice rock avalanches ever recorded, on the Nepal-China border – it killed thousands of people and left damage equivalent to 10% of Nepal’s GDP in a single event,” said Kirkham. “Switzerland has lost 20% of its glacier ice in the last five years, and thousands of glaciers worldwide are expected to become extinct in the coming decade, every single year.”

Bill Hare, a climate scientist and the CEO of Climate Analytics, a policy institute, who was not involved in the report, said: “Ice sheets melting six times faster than 30 years ago, sea ice and mountain glaciers disappearing at record speed, sea levels inexorably rising, the life-giving polar oceans acidifying: all irreversible now on human timescales, all laden with worldwide consequences, and all taking climate impacts past limits of adaptability.”

He added: “Every government minister and every fossil fuel executive who’s ever succeeded in watering down climate action can look at this report and see how their actions have fundamentally damaged the world we live in.”
output.standfirst: Keeping long-term warming to around 0.8C could preserve most of the world's glaciers, a UN-backed report finds, but even if warming is capped at 1.5C, mountain glaciers in regions such as the Rockies, Alps, Iceland and Scandinavia could lose up to 80% of their mass, and permafrost and ice sheets would suffer lasting harm
output.progress: World leaders are meeting at Cop31 in Turkey as scientists call for deeper emissions cuts to limit the damage.

output.headline: Mahmood set to exempt care workers from toughest new settlement rules
output.bodyHtml:
Care workers already in the UK are expected to be spared the toughest new settlement rules when Shabana Mahmood announces them on Monday, even as most other legal migrants will have to wait a decade, and some up to 15 years, for the right to settle permanently.

Mahmood, the home secretary, has proposed that the settlement wait could be reduced if legal migrants showed they had contributed to their local communities via a “points based system”, or if they were earning higher incomes.

She is expected to meet union general secretaries on Monday – some of whom have raised alarm at the changes – to map out the final details.

The Guardian first reported in July that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was considering exempting hundreds of thousands of care workers from the reforms to relieve pressure on the social care sector. The Home Office has granted about 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more people coming as their dependants.

Ministers – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner – had raised concerns about the effect the rules would have on care workers already in the UK, who would otherwise face a 15-year wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR).

Under the plans published for consultation, the standard qualifying period for settlement would double from five to 10 years, while some workers in occupations below graduate level, including care workers, could face a 15-year qualifying period, subject to the proposed exemptions and reductions.

In June, Rayner described making care workers already in Britain wait up to 15 years for permanent residence as “un-British”. In September, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the plans would have been “tough” for her family, who came to Britain as refugees.

In a letter to Mahmood and the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, seen by the Guardian, parliamentarians and organisations representing migrant workers, racial equality campaigners and health professionals describe the proposals as “an iteration of Windrush era policies”.

The Windrush scandal, exposed by Guardian reporting in 2017, involved mainly Black Britons being wrongly detained, deported and denied access to work and essential services, despite having the right to live in Britain.

In their letter, dated 29 October, the signatories urge ministers to “stop history from repeating itself” by abandoning the proposals or, at a minimum, introducing extra safeguards.

They warn that the proposed exemptions for some public-service workers may fail to protect staff employed by independent health and social care providers, as well as workers’ family members.

Signatories argue that changing the rules for people who have planned their lives around existing settlement requirements would be unfair, and could encourage essential workers to leave the country.

The letter urges ministers to follow the recommendations of the Windrush Lessons Learned Review, conducted by Wendy Williams, which called for improvements in the development and scrutiny of immigration policy, including greater consideration of its impact on affected communities.

The signatories warn the health and care sector is already “dangerously under-staffed”, and that the proposed changes risk “worsening the health and wellbeing of everyone in the UK”.

The letter argues that the government could struggle to meet cancer treatment and NHS waiting-list reduction targets without retaining and expanding the workforce, particularly in professions heavily reliant on internationally trained staff, such as radiography.

It raises particular concerns about adult social care, adding: “International workers are essential to maintaining current levels of care. Without them, services will contract, and unmet need will increase.”

The signatories write: “Windrush was a scandal borne from racist immigration policies … this situation is not historic when this same wrong persists, and the same groups are targeted by current immigration proposals.”

The Labour MPs Bell Ribeiro-Addy, Diane Abbott, Clive Lewis and Rachael Maskell are among the signatories, alongside the Green MPs Ellie Chowns, Carla Denyer, Siân Berry and Hannah Spencer. Organisations backing the letter include the Work Rights Centre, Action for Race Equality, Care England and the Society of Radiographers.

Launching the consultation on earned settlement last year, Mahmood described Britain as a “multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy” that demanded “contribution and integration”. She added: “To become a part of this country, permanently, is therefore not a right but a privilege – and one that must be earned.”
output.standfirst: Care workers already in the UK are expected to be spared the harshest new wait for settlement, as other legal migrants face waits of up to 15 years under rules ministers will set out on Monday
output.progress: Mahmood is expected to exempt care workers from the longest waits and meets union leaders on Monday to finalise the plans.

output.headline: Hoisted by his rivals, Antonelli completes record-breaking title charge
output.bodyHtml:
Kimi Antonelli was hoisted on to the shoulders of Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen on the Mexico City podium, tears of joy marking the moment the 20-year-old became Formula One's youngest world champion, and the first Italian to take the crown since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

The title also ends a six-year wait for Mercedes, who last won the drivers' championship with Hamilton in 2020, and the team's 10th drivers' title overall. Antonelli, promoted into Hamilton's old seat only last season after a difficult rookie year, sealed it with third place at the Mexican Grand Prix, a race won by Red Bull's Verstappen from Hamilton's Ferrari, with Hamilton's teammate Charles Leclerc fourth.

Related: ‘He’s done an insane job’: Antonelli’s rivals united in praise for ‘incredible’ champion

Antonelli said the day would live with him for ever but had left him almost speechless. His race engineer, Peter Bonnington, said: “It is a very special day, a young man has broken the record for the youngest world champion. It is the first of many I reckon, I am just super happy for him, stoked.”

He becomes the sport's 36th world champion, in only his second F1 season, with four races still to go. Sebastian Vettel had been the previous youngest champion, aged 23 in 2010, when Antonelli was four.

Antonelli has led since taking the lead after the third round in Japan, and made the most of an early-season Mercedes advantage under the new regulations, winning five of the first six races and outracing his teammate George Russell, the pre-season favourite. He went on to take nine wins, failing to score points only twice, both times through mechanical failures, and held his lead even as Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull pushed Mercedes hard, including a win from 19th on the grid at his home race in Monza.

Russell and Hamilton, his nearest rivals, needed to win in Mexico to keep the title race alive, but Antonelli's third place would have clinched it regardless. He qualified only fourth but delivered what he needed — ninth place or better — with a nerveless drive true to his season's form.

The race itself was a feisty affair. Leclerc made a strong start and tried to pass Hamilton for the lead at turn four but cut the corner to do it, and did not give the place back; stewards investigated and handed him a five-second penalty, to be served in his pit stop, for gaining an advantage by leaving the track. Hamilton, left furious that his teammate had cost them a one-two finish and let Verstappen through to the lead, said: “The problem is he's got clean air and doesn't have to manage like the rest of us. He should just give the place back. The stewards are basically handing Charles this win.” Later, as the race was stopped, he added: “We've got big problems. Big, big problems.” A lively debrief awaits at Ferrari.

A red flag followed a heavy crash for Valtteri Bottas at turn one. The restart saw Hamilton move up to second and Antonelli to third — not one to settle quietly for the minimum needed, he went on to seal the title with a podium finish, where Hamilton and Verstappen lifted him on to their shoulders.

Related: Kimi Antonelli claims the Formula One crown – his season in pictures

Verstappen's own drive from fifth on the grid was hugely impressive, and should buoy Red Bull heading into next season, setting up the prospect of him, Antonelli and, hopefully, Hamilton competing consistently at the front in 2027 — some consolation after missing out on the title himself.

For Mercedes, the win vindicates the faith the team placed in Antonelli, brought into their young driver programme at 12 and thrown into Hamilton's seat last year. He has adapted to Formula One's sharp end with alacrity and skill since, and after a season on top from start to finish, this fascinating, precocious talent looks unlikely to be done winning yet.
output.standfirst:
• 20-year-old seals title with third place and four races to spare

  • Verstappen wins race ahead of Hamilton
output.progress: Antonelli sealed the title with four races still to run, ending Mercedes' six-year wait for the drivers' championship.

output.headline: Oleshky ceasefire hailed a success as families reunite
output.bodyHtml:
A six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, came to an end on Sunday night, after hundreds of residents were reunited with their loved ones in northern Ukraine, with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success. Separately, Ukraine's raids on Russian oil refineries, in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, had already restarted on Friday.

“The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended,” said Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, hailing what had been an “important step in our joint humanitarian efforts”.

Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.

The Wall Street Journal had reported that Ukraine had given in to pressure from the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper that they never agreed to a demand from Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on Russia restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv was now “simply ignoring” US wishes.

Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.

Related: Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce shows de-escalation is possible, says Zelenskyy

Zelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he said, as part of Ukraine’s continuing “long-range sanctions”.

Zelenskyy said his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four Ukrainian regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.

“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram. Kyiv experienced power cuts lasting eight to 10 hours on Sunday after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.

Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sqkm (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sqkm (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”

Ukrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleshky. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.

The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would pave the way for broader peace efforts.

“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.

Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, and Kremlin officials said on Sunday that Vladimir Putin was willing to talk directly to Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.

There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged.

He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces, which the Kremlin does not control but says it has “annexed”.
output.standfirst: The six-day truce in Oleshky reunited hundreds of families and was hailed by both sides as a humanitarian success, as Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries in defiance of Donald Trump ahead of the US midterms.
output.progress: Ukraine's ombudsman hails the Oleshky ceasefire a humanitarian success; separately, Kremlin officials say Putin is willing to speak directly to Zelenskyy, with trilateral talks likely later this month.

output.headline: Iran shortens Hormuz reopening timetable as Qatar-brokered talks reach third day
output.bodyHtml:
Indirect talks mediated by Qatar in Doha reached a third day on Sunday, as negotiators worked to secure the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets — a move that could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.

In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.

Officials from the Gulf states remain ‘braced for the worst’ as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.

The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: ‘We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.’

He added: ‘Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.’

Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose ‘diplomacy over other paths’. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s ‘rationality’. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.

Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.

Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.

Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in ‘tone’ from the US side but said he had yet to respond.

Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.

Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to ‘take care of’ one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were ‘going fine but you know they’re not very reliable’.

Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: ‘Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.’

Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: ‘Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.’
output.standfirst: Iran has agreed to compress its Hormuz reopening timetable from seven days to two, even as Gulf officials remain ‘braced for the worst’ days after a missile strike hit a tanker near the strait.
output.progress: Qatar is mediating between Washington and Tehran, and Iran has agreed to compress its reopening timetable for the strait of Hormuz from seven days to two.

output.headline: Sofia Demetriades crowned BBC Young Musician after dazzling Tchaikovsky performance
output.bodyHtml:
Sofia Demetriades, an 18-year-old violinist from Leicestershire, has won the BBC Young Musician competition 2026, in the first all-female final in the competition's 48-year history.

The judges, Joanna MacGregor, Ben Gernon and Errollyn Wallen, hailed Demetriades's performance of Tchaikovsky's Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity.

She is in her first year of undergraduate studies at the Royal Academy of Music.

The brainchild of Humphrey Burton, the biennial BBC competition was set up in 1978 and has produced finalists such as Sheku Kanneh-Mason, Alison Balsom, Stephen Hough and, in 2004, Nicola Benedetti, who was the last violinist to win.

Demetriades was one of several hundred to send in a video application, before 40 young players were selected to attend live auditions at Bath Spa University to gain one of eight places in the quarter-finals – which took place on Demetriades's 18th birthday. Among her fellow quarter-finalists was the first accordion player to reach the final stages, 14-year-old Sylvester Maschi.

Each of the three finalists performed a concerto with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales, conducted by Alpesh Chauhan in a concert at Bristol Beacon. An 18-year-old saxophone player, Kezia Colton, performed Takashi Yoshimatsu's 1994 Cyber Bird Saxophone Concerto, while 17-year-old recorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni played Graham Fitkin's Recorder Concerto.

Fitkin's virtuosic concerto involves six different recorders, ranging from the giant contrabass, about 1.6 metres high, to the tiniest sopranino. It was originally commissioned by Debretzeni's teacher, Barbara Law, and it was given its premiere performance in 2017 by 2014's Young Musician finalist, Sophie Westbrooke. And there was a further connection this year to previous competitions – 2022's overall winner, the percussionist Jordan Ashman, joined Kezia Colton onstage for Yoshimatsu's concerto.

Wallen praised Colton's playing: "Kezia plays with incredible verve and spirit." Gernon added: "Her performance was sassy and cool, but her more intimate playing is incredibly strong too."

The judges hailed the "electricity, aliveness, and beautiful intensity" that Debretzeni brought to Fitkin's concerto. Wallen said: "She took us on a musical journey … we were inside every note."

Debretzeni said the experience had changed her plans: "Before the competition I hadn't planned on being a musician. I wanted to study psychology … but this has been so inspiring it's made me want to pursue music. It's been literally life-changing."

MacGregor acclaimed Demetriades as a simply extraordinary musician: "She performs with her eyes, achieving dizzying technical feats but she looks as if she's enjoying it."

"Sofia's innate sense of colour, musical style and architecture combines with an effortless technique, and a joy for whatever music she's playing," MacGregor said. "In a competition full of gifted and dedicated young musicians, Sofia's sensitivity and sophistication stood out in every round. I'm very excited to watch her musicianship develop even further in the years ahead."

The winner receives the trophy, a cash prize of £3,000 towards music studies as well as recording and broadcast opportunities on Radio 3, including with one of the BBC ensembles. All three finalists will work with Young Classical Artists Trust on managing their future careers.

Demetriades said she was thrilled by the win: "I am so honoured and thrilled to have been a part of BBC Young Musician. I loved playing in the quarter-final on my 18th birthday. I didn't think I could top that, but to go on to be crowned winner is my absolute dream! It was pure delight to share the stage with BBC NOW, Alpesh Chauhan and my fellow finalists – I really hope to play alongside them again soon."

• The final and the three previous stages are available to watch on BBC iPlayer
output.standfirst: The 18-year-old violinist's performance of Tchaikovsky's Violin Concerto in the competition's first all-female final was hailed by judges as full of insight, poetry and maturity
